title-group.article-title: Longitudinal patient-reported fatigue during adjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer.

contrib-group.aff: Southern Clinical Oncology Center, Atlanta, GA
Pacific Precision Medicine Institute, San Francisco, CA
Great Lakes Cancer Consortium, Detroit, MI

abstract.p: Background: Patient-reported fatigue is common among patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, but its trajectory during and after treatment is not consistently captured in routine oncology practice. We characterized longitudinal symptom burden and factors associated with clinically meaningful worsening. Methods: Participants completed the PROMIS Fatigue Short Form at baseline, cycle 2, end of treatment, and 3 months after treatment. Mixed-effects models evaluated change over time, and multivariable regression assessed baseline clinical and patient-reported predictors. A prespecified threshold was used to define clinically meaningful worsening from baseline. Results: The cohort included 214 patients. Mean symptom score was 51.2 at baseline, reached 60.8 at the period of greatest burden, and was 54.1 at the final assessment. Clinically meaningful worsening occurred in 48% of participants. In adjusted analysis, baseline sleep disturbance was independently associated with worse longitudinal symptom scores (β=0.31, p=<0.001). Completion rates exceeded 80% at each scheduled assessment. Conclusions: Fatigue changed substantially over the treatment course among patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer. Routine longitudinal assessment may identify patients who would benefit from earlier supportive care, particularly those with baseline sleep disturbance. Research Sponsor: None.
